hypothesis: If all living things share a common chemistry, cellular machinery and growth/reproduction processes, then a substantial set of orthologous protein families (the molecular basis of that shared machinery) will be present in nearly every genome, including genomes from the two prokaryotic domains, bacteria and archaea.
pass_criterion: Using the COG2024 genome-by-COG presence/absence data (2,103 bacterial and 193 archaeal genomes), at least 50 COGs are each present in at least 90% of all genomes. At least 20 of those COGs must also be present in at least 90% of the archaeal genomes and at least 90% of the bacterial genomes when each domain is counted separately. The COGs must include categories J (translation), K (transcription) and L (replication) so that they cover growth and reproduction machinery.
fail_criterion: Fewer than 10 COGs are present in at least 90% of all genomes, or fewer than 5 COGs are present in at least 90% of both the bacterial and the archaeal genomes. Either result means no substantial shared molecular core, so the claim is refuted at this scope. Results between these bounds (10-49 COGs, or 5-19 cross-domain) are inconclusive.
interpretation: Darwin's 'chemical composition', 'cellular structure' and 'laws of growth and reproduction' are mapped to the conserved protein-coding gene families that carry out core chemistry and cell processes: translation, transcription, replication, and central metabolism. 'All living things' is restricted to the cellular organisms in this dataset, which are bacteria and archaea. Eukaryotes are not covered, so this tests the claim only within that scope and cannot confirm it for plants and animals. 'Germinal vesicles' and 'the same poison affecting plants and animals' are not directly measurable here; conserved protein targets are a modern proxy for the poison argument. The 90% presence threshold allows for annotation gaps and for reduced genomes such as endosymbionts.

dataset.name: COG - NCBI (Database of Clusters of Orthologous Genes, COG2024 release)
dataset.publisher: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), US National Library of Medicine
dataset.why_it_fits: The landing page describes the COG2024 release covering 2,103 bacterial and 193 archaeal species and links to an FTP data folder (https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/COG/COG2024/data/). The page does not list individual filenames or fields. The planned analysis uses the COG-to-protein assignment tables and the COG definition file with its functional-category letters, and computes the fraction of genomes containing each COG, overall and by domain. I have not confirmed the exact file names; they must be read from the FTP folder before analysis. The page shows no DOI for the dataset, so none is given.
